title: Orchestrate durable AI workflows with Azure Durable Functions

questions.q: An orchestrator needs to call a classification model for each document. Where should the model call go?

options.text: Directly in the orchestrator
options.why: Orchestrators must stay deterministic and avoid external calls.

options.text: In an activity function
options.why: Correct. Activities perform nondeterministic work such as model calls.

options.text: In the client function
options.why: Clients start and manage orchestrations.

options.text: In an entity function
options.why: Entities manage small pieces of durable state.

questions.hint: Orchestrators coordinate. The function type that does real I/O is a different one.
questions.explain: The orchestrator schedules activities and records only their results.

questions.q: Which API gives an orchestrator a replay-safe current time?

options.text: datetime.now() in Python
options.why: Language-native time APIs change between replays.

options.text: context.current_utc_datetime
options.why: Correct. It returns the same value during replay.

options.text: time.time() from the time module
options.why: Nondeterministic across replays.

options.text: datetime.utcnow() in Python
options.why: Nondeterministic across replays.

questions.hint: The context object gives you a time value that's the same on every replay.
questions.explain: Use context.current_utc_datetime and context.new_uuid() in orchestrators.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A developer reviews an orchestrator function.

rows.text: Using time.sleep(60) to pause between steps is acceptable.
rows.why: Blocking waits aren't allowed; use durable timers.

rows.text: Branching on the result returned by an activity is acceptable.
rows.why: Results of durable tasks are safe inputs to decisions.

rows.text: Calling uuid.uuid4() for an operation ID is acceptable.
rows.why: Use context.new_uuid() for a deterministic identifier.

rows.text: Passing a blob URL instead of the whole document to an activity is recommended.
rows.why: Pass references to keep history small.

questions.hint: No sleeping, no random IDs in the orchestrator. Branching on results is fine.
questions.explain: Orchestrators coordinate deterministically; activities do the I/O.

questions.q: Logs show the same "Starting classification" orchestrator message five times for one workflow, although the activity ran once. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: The client started five orchestrations; use a fixed instance ID
options.why: One instance replaying explains this.

options.text: Application Insights duplicates logs; turn off sampling for it
options.why: Duplicates come from replay, not sampling.

options.text: The activity ran five times; add a retry policy to it
options.why: The activity ran once; the duplicates come from replay.

options.text: Replay reruns the log line; check context.is_replaying
options.why: Correct. Replay can run orchestrator log statements again.

questions.hint: Orchestrator code runs more than once. Is there a way to tell when it's running again?
questions.explain: Activity logs reflect real work; orchestrator logs can repeat during replay.

questions.q: Orchestrations that pass full extracted text and model responses between steps have become slow, and history storage is growing. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Move the model calls into the orchestrator to avoid passing data
options.why: Model calls in the orchestrator break determinism.

options.text: Switch the storage provider to Azure Storage
options.why: The provider choice doesn't fix oversized history.

options.text: Store content in Blob Storage; pass references
options.why: Correct. Large payloads increase storage operations, replay time and memory.

options.text: Compress the payloads inside the orchestrator with a random salt
options.why: Random values don't belong in orchestrators, and the payload stays in history.

questions.hint: Everything passed between steps is saved in history. Keep it small.
questions.explain: Activities read and write large content; orchestrators get IDs, URLs and scores.

questions.q: You're starting a new Durable Functions application and choosing a storage provider. Which one does Microsoft recommend for new apps?

options.text: The Azure Storage provider
options.why: It's still available for existing apps or when you want to manage storage yourself, but it isn't the recommendation for new apps.

options.text: Azure Cache for Redis
options.why: Redis isn't a Durable Functions storage provider.

options.text: Azure Cosmos DB as a custom provider
options.why: Learn's recommendation for new apps is the managed Durable Task Scheduler.

options.text: Durable Task Scheduler
options.why: Correct. It's the recommended managed storage provider for new Durable Functions apps.

questions.hint: Microsoft now offers a managed backend built specifically for durable task state.
questions.explain: For new Durable Functions applications, Microsoft recommends Durable Task Scheduler as the managed storage provider. The Azure Storage provider remains for existing apps or self-managed storage.

questions.q: An orchestrator passes a model API key to each activity as part of the activity input, so that activities can call the model. What's wrong with this design?

options.text: Activities can't receive string inputs
options.why: Activities take serializable inputs, including strings.

options.text: The key makes the orchestrator non-deterministic
options.why: The key is the same every time. The problem is where it's stored.

options.text: Inputs are saved in orchestration history, so the key is stored there; use managed identity and Key Vault instead
options.why: Correct. Don't place secrets in orchestration inputs or outputs.

options.text: Nothing, as long as the key is rotated every month
options.why: Rotation helps, but the secret would still be kept in durable history.

questions.hint: Think about where Durable Functions keeps inputs and outputs.
questions.explain: Orchestration inputs and outputs are serialized into durable history. Don't put secrets, access tokens or model credentials there; use managed identities and a service such as Azure Key Vault.

questions.q: An orchestrator must classify 20 independent images in parallel and then summarise. What should it do?

options.text: Yield each call_activity in a loop, one after another
options.why: Yielding each call immediately runs them sequentially.

options.text: Create 20 tasks, then yield task_all
options.why: Correct. Schedule all tasks first, then wait for the group.

options.text: Call the model 20 times directly in the orchestrator
options.why: Model calls belong in activities.

options.text: Start 20 separate client functions
options.why: Clients start orchestrations; this is fan-out inside one orchestration.

questions.hint: Start all the work before you wait for any of it.
questions.explain: Fan-out: create tasks without yielding; fan-in: yield task_all.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An orchestrator yields `context.task_all(tasks)` for five document tasks, and task 3 finishes first.

rows.text: The result list has task 3's result first.
rows.why: Results match the order of the task list.

rows.text: If one activity fails, task_all surfaces a failure to the orchestrator.
rows.why: The orchestrator can then fail, compensate or route the batch.

rows.text: Each activity should return the full extracted text for aggregation.
rows.why: Return compact fields and a result URL.

questions.hint: Results come back in task order. One failure surfaces. Keep outputs small.
questions.explain: Ordered results, explicit failure handling, compact outputs.

questions.q: A batch of 10,000 documents fans out all at once and the model endpoint starts throttling. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Return the model responses to the orchestrator to retry them there
options.why: Large responses bloat history and retries belong to activities.

options.text: Increase the function app's instance memory to 4,096 MB
options.why: Memory doesn't change the model's rate limits.

options.text: Process bounded batches, one batch at a time
options.why: Correct. Bounded batches limit scheduled work to fit downstream quotas.

options.text: Add time.sleep() between activity calls in the orchestrator
options.why: Never sleep in an orchestrator; use durable timers if a pause is needed.

questions.hint: Too much at once hits quotas. Limit how many run together.
questions.explain: Choose batch size from model quotas, item duration and concurrency.

questions.q: A claim archive of a million documents makes one orchestrator's fan-in a bottleneck. Which design helps?

options.text: Running all aggregation inside the client function
options.why: Clients manage orchestrations; they don't aggregate durable results.

options.text: A parent with sub-orchestrations per partition
options.why: Correct. Each child handles a partition and returns counts and locations.

options.text: Removing fan-in and letting activities write a shared counter
options.why: Shared counters lose the durable coordination.

options.text: One orchestrator that loads every individual result for aggregation
options.why: That's the bottleneck being fixed.

questions.hint: One orchestrator can only aggregate so much. Split the work into child orchestrations.
questions.explain: Introduce sub-orchestrations when batch size or aggregation cost justifies them.

questions.q: An orchestration must wait up to 48 hours for an adjuster's decision, then take a timeout path. What should it use?

options.text: An activity that blocks until the adjuster answers
options.why: An activity would hold a worker for days.

options.text: A loop that polls the approval table every minute
options.why: Polling from the orchestrator is inefficient; events resume it.

options.text: task_any() racing the event against a timer
options.why: Correct. Whichever completes first decides the path.

options.text: time.sleep() for 48 hours, then check the database
options.why: Blocking waits aren't allowed in orchestrators.

questions.hint: Wait for an event or a deadline, whichever comes first.
questions.explain: Human interaction pattern: wait_for_external_event + create_timer + task_any.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An approval orchestration races an ApprovalResponse event against a 48-hour timer.

rows.text: The suspended orchestration holds a worker for the full 48 hours.
rows.why: It doesn't hold a worker or active invocation while waiting.

rows.text: If the event wins, the orchestrator should cancel the pending timer.
rows.why: Every pending timer must be waited for or cancelled before exit.

rows.text: An event sent before the orchestrator starts waiting is lost.
rows.why: Early events are persisted and consumed later.

rows.text: Knowing the instance ID is enough proof that the caller may approve.
rows.why: Authenticate and authorize callers; the ID is just an address.

questions.hint: Waiting costs almost nothing. Cancel the timer you didn't need, and secure the endpoint.
questions.explain: Durable waits are cheap, but endpoints must still be secured.

questions.q: A reviewer double-clicks Approve and two ApprovalResponse events arrive; a stale review link also sends an old decision. How should the workflow cope?

options.text: Accept whichever of the events arrives last
options.why: Arrival order alone isn't a reliable policy.

options.text: Accept every event and create one approval record for each
options.why: Duplicates would create duplicate approvals.

options.text: Use request ID and version; record the first valid decision once
options.why: Correct. Versioned, idempotent recording handles duplicates and out-of-order responses.

options.text: Turn off at-least-once delivery for the external events
options.why: At-least-once delivery isn't something you switch off.

questions.hint: Expect duplicates and old decisions.
questions.explain: Design for duplicates and stale responses explicitly.

questions.q: A client function raises the ApprovalResponse event after authorizing the reviewer. What should its HTTP response be?

options.text: 204 No Content after the orchestration completes
options.why: The client doesn't wait for completion.

options.text: 409 Conflict
options.why: Nothing conflicts in the normal path.

options.text: 202 Accepted
options.why: Correct. Event delivery resumes the orchestration asynchronously.

options.text: 200 OK with the final claim result
options.why: The final result isn't available yet.

questions.hint: Raising an event is asynchronous, so don't promise the outcome yet.
questions.explain: Raising an event is asynchronous; return 202 and let callers track status.

questions.q: An HTTP-triggered client function receives a reviewer's approval for orchestration instance claim-482. Which call delivers it to the waiting orchestration?

options.text: client.start_new("approval", instance_id, data)
options.why: start_new starts a new instance. It doesn't deliver an event to a running one.

options.text: client.terminate(instance_id, "approved")
options.why: terminate stops the orchestration instead of letting it continue.

options.text: context.wait_for_external_event("ApprovalResponse")
options.why: That's what the orchestrator calls to wait. A client function can't use it.

options.text: client.raise_event(instance_id, "ApprovalResponse", data)
options.why: Correct. raise_event sends a named external event to that instance, and the name must match what the orchestrator waits for.

questions.hint: The orchestrator waits for a named event. Which client method sends one?
questions.explain: A client function uses raise_event(instance_id, event_name, data) to send a named external event to a specific instance. The orchestrator waits with wait_for_external_event(name).

questions.q: A caller starts a long document workflow over HTTP and needs a way to check its progress later. What does Learn say an HTTP-triggered client function often returns?

options.text: The final result, after waiting for the orchestration to finish
options.why: Long workflows would hit HTTP timeouts. The client returns quickly with tracking information.

options.text: The orchestrator's replay history
options.why: History is internal state, not something to hand to callers.

options.text: Status URLs that the caller can use to track the workflow
options.why: Correct. Client functions start orchestrations and often return status URLs for long-running workflows.

options.text: A function key for the orchestrator
options.why: Keys don't track progress, and you shouldn't give them out this way.

questions.hint: The work takes a long time. What lets the caller come back and ask how it's going?
questions.explain: Client functions start orchestrations, query status, terminate them and send external events. An HTTP-triggered client often returns status URLs for tracking a long-running workflow.

questions.q: Match each failure to the handling Learn recommends.

items.text: The model endpoint returns a throttling response
The upload is an unsupported content type
items.why: Permanent failures won't succeed on retry.

items.text: Classification confidence is below the threshold

questions.hint: Throttling is transient, bad input is terminal, and low confidence is a business rule.
questions.explain: Classify failures before retrying.

questions.q: An activity writes a result blob, then the host crashes before the result is recorded, so the activity runs again. How should it avoid a duplicate?

options.text: Generate a new uuid.uuid4() blob name on each attempt
options.why: A new ID per attempt makes each retry look like new work.

options.text: Name the blob with a stable operation ID; skip if present
options.why: Correct. The retry recognizes the existing result and returns the same URL.

options.text: Write the result from the orchestrator instead of the activity
options.why: Orchestrators must not do I/O.

options.text: Disable retries for the activity so it can't run twice
options.why: Retries are needed for transient failures.

questions.hint: The write must land in the same place every time the activity runs.
questions.explain: Pass an operation ID (from input or context.new_uuid()) for idempotent writes.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A step races a processing activity against a 10-minute durable timer, and the timer wins.

rows.text: The running activity is cancelled automatically.
rows.why: A winning timer doesn't cancel a started activity.

rows.text: The workflow should ignore a late result after its terminal deadline.
rows.why: Design to ignore late results and keep writes idempotent.

rows.text: A model-call timeout means the whole claim must be marked invalid.
rows.why: Choose the narrowest timeout; retry, fall back or send to manual review.

questions.hint: A timer winning doesn't stop work already started.
questions.explain: Timeouts bound waiting; they don't undo work already in flight.

questions.q: Document processing exhausts its retries after a provisional summary was published. What should the orchestrator do?

options.text: Retry the activity forever until it finally succeeds
options.why: Retries must be bounded.

options.text: Delete every audit record of the provisional summary
options.why: Preserve audit evidence; compensation is a new business action.

options.text: Run an idempotent compensation activity, then rethrow
options.why: Correct. Compensate the earlier side effect and keep a Failed terminal status.

options.text: Catch the exception and report the workflow as Completed
options.why: Hiding the failure misreports the outcome.

questions.hint: Retries are exhausted. Undo what was published, then fail honestly.
questions.explain: Compensation addresses completed side effects without pretending to roll back.

questions.q: An activity should run at most 3 times, waiting 5 seconds before the first retry. Which Python code is correct?

options.text: context.call_activity("Classify", df.RetryOptions(5_000, 3), doc)
options.why: Plain call_activity doesn't apply a retry policy.

options.text: context.call_activity_with_retry("Classify", df.RetryOptions(5_000, 3), doc)
options.why: Correct. RetryOptions takes the first retry interval in milliseconds, then the max number of attempts.

options.text: context.call_activity_with_retry("Classify", df.RetryOptions(3, 5_000), doc)
options.why: The arguments are swapped: that's a 3 ms first interval and 5,000 attempts.

options.text: context.call_activity_with_retry("Classify", df.RetryOptions(5, 3), doc)
options.why: The interval is in milliseconds, so 5 means 5 ms, not 5 seconds.

questions.hint: Check the units of the first argument, and which call accepts a retry policy.
questions.explain: df.RetryOptions(first_retry_interval_in_milliseconds, max_number_of_attempts) is used with context.call_activity_with_retry().

questions.q: A retried activity creates its operation ID with uuid.uuid4(), and duplicate result blobs appear. What's the best fix?

options.text: Create the ID in the orchestrator with context.new_uuid() and pass it to the activity
options.why: Correct. The ID stays the same across retries and replays, so repeated writes land in the same place.

options.text: Write the result blob with overwrite=True
options.why: With a new ID each time, each retry writes a different blob, so overwriting doesn't help.

options.text: Lower the retry policy to a single attempt
options.why: Activities can still run more than once, and you lose resilience.

options.text: Call uuid.uuid4() in the orchestrator and pass it in
options.why: uuid4 in an orchestrator gives a new value on each replay, which breaks determinism.

questions.hint: The ID has to be the same every time the step runs, and that includes replays.
questions.explain: Activities run at least once, so the operation ID must be stable. Create it deterministically in the orchestrator with context.new_uuid() (or derive it from input) and pass it to the activity.
